raw_evidence.label: The 'manager myth' in popular football discourse
raw_evidence.content: Football culture treats managers as decisive, almost mystical figures. Pundits credit promoted teams' survival to a 'manager bounce', clubs sack coaches mid-season hoping for an instant lift, and TV cameras linger on the touchline as if the man pacing there is shaping every kick. Academic work has long pushed back: studies of Bundesliga and Premier League sackings find that the post-firing improvement most clubs experience is largely regression to the mean — bad runs would have ended anyway. The Economist's framing — that managers matter 'much less than most fans think' — sits inside this longer revisionist tradition that says squad quality, not the suit on the touchline, drives most of what happens.

raw_evidence.content: The model lets you compare a coach and a player on the same scale: points added per season above an average peer. The best projected manager (Favre) is worth +3.76. Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi each rate +9.24 — about 2.46 times the impact of the best coach in the data. In other words, replacing a typical attacker with Messi at a mid-table side moves the team further up the table than swapping that side's manager for the very best one available.

# --- ana_06: Squad strength dwarfs manager — Messi worth 9.2 vs Favre 3.76 ---
print("\n=== ana_06 ===")
top_mgr = managers["ProjPointsAboveAverage"].max()
top_player = players["PointsAboveAverage"].max()
top_player_name = players.loc[players["PointsAboveAverage"].idxmax(), "FIFA_player_name"]
print(f"Best projected manager (per season): +{top_mgr:.2f} pts")
print(f"Best single player ({top_player_name}): +{top_player:.2f} pts/season")
print(f"Top player worth {top_player/top_mgr:.2f}x the top manager")
# Top 10 attackers and goalkeepers
att = players[players["PosGroup"] == "attack"].sort_values("PointsAboveAverage", ascending=False).head(5)
gk = players[players["PosGroup"] == "goalkeeper"].sort_values("PointsAboveAverage", ascending=False).head(5)
print("Top attackers:")
for _, r in att.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['FIFA_player_name']:<30s} +{r['PointsAboveAverage']:.2f} pts/season")
print("Top goalkeepers:")
for _, r in gk.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['FIFA_player_name']:<30s} +{r['PointsAboveAverage']:.2f} pts/season")

raw_evidence.content: The 596 currently employed top-flight managers in the dataset are projected to add a median of -0.36 points per season relative to an average coach, with a standard deviation of 0.84. Even at the extremes the spread is only 6.56 points: the best projected manager is +3.76 (Lucien Favre), the worst -2.80. By contrast a single elite player can shift a team's points total by more than 9. Most coaches sit in a narrow band, and almost none of them — even projected — clear the influence of one good attacker.

print(f"Mean: {m.mean():.3f}")

raw_evidence.content: EA Sports' FIFA series produces an annual snapshot of every top-flight player's ability, scored 0–99, blending objective stats (passes, tackles, shots) with subjective evaluations from roughly 9,000 dedicated scouts. The worst regular starters in top divisions sit around 65; legends like Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo can reach 94. Because FIFA's ratings are set before each season — independent of that year's results — they are a rare publicly available estimate of player skill that does not bake in team performance. The Economist team z-scored players within position groups and applied an exponent so that elite ability counts more than middling ability, then summed exponentiated z-scores for each squad's first-choice goalkeeper, top five defenders, and top seven attackers.

raw_evidence.label: Why the goalkeeper coefficient is small
raw_evidence.content: When the regression learned how each positional group affects winning, drawing and losing, the coefficients for attackers and defenders were similarly large — but goalkeepers' coefficient was very small. That matches independent work by 21st Club, a football consultancy, which estimated that even the best goalkeepers add only about four points per season to an average team — much less than the best attackers. In the Economist model, swapping an average attacker for Lionel Messi at a mid-table side like Celta Vigo improves the team by roughly 9.2 points a season; goalkeepers can't move the dial nearly that much.
